captions.instagram:
What are acids and bases?

Lemon juice has about 20,000 times more hydrogen ions than milk, and one drop can swing a flask from pH 4 to pH 10. Solve real pH from real equilibrium constants, run a titration, watch a haldi stain turn red, see why blood stays at 7.4, and test what alkaline water really does to stomach acid.

→ An acid gives hydrogen ions to water. Each step down the pH scale means ten times more of them.
→ Vinegar’s acid is weak: at 0.1 mol/L only 1 molecule in 76 lets go, so its pH is 2.9, not 1.
→ Battery acid, lemon, curd, milk, blood, soap, bleach: every step along the shelf is ten times.
→ Rub soap on a haldi stain and it turns red. Turmeric is a pH indicator.
→ Add base to acid drop by drop. For 24 millilitres almost nothing happens. Then one drop flips it.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/acidbaseclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: What are acids and bases? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Lemon juice has about 20,000 times more hydrogen ions than milk, and one drop can swing a flask from pH 4 to pH 10. Solve real pH from real equilibrium constants, run a titration, watch a haldi stain turn red, see why blood stays at 7.4, and test what alkaline water really does to stomach acid.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/acidbaseclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/acidbaseclear

In this video:
• The pH scale. An acid gives a proton to water, making H₃O⁺; a base takes one, leaving OH⁻.
• Around the house. Lemon juice is about pH 2.3, curd 4.6, milk 6.6, blood 7.4, baking soda 8.3, soap 9 to 10, bleach about 12.5.
• Neutralisation. Acid plus base gives a salt and water.
• Buffers, blood, teeth and rain. A weak acid mixed with its salt soaks up added acid or base.
• Limits and a myth. pH can go below 0 and above 14.
